fine: Su et al. 2021; Chen et al. 2023; bloc97 2023; Peng et al. 2023; Hsieh et al. 2024.
Two clips are from her lecture 4 recap. The narration is a synthetic voice.
title: RoPE
Position as a Rotation
en.turnS: a pair of numbers from the query or the key = one arrow
en.same5: the angle between them: the same
en.distS: a score = how well two arrows line up (their dot product)
en.only6: only the words and their distance
en.nox: times q and k: no cross terms
en.qk: turns the queries and the keys; the values are not turned
en.clkS: Llama 2's smallest model: 128 numbers per head
en.seen: in training: at most about 27 degrees
en.fix: the fix: slow the clocks down
en.piS: Chen et al., 2023: every clock slower by the same factor
en.bk2: to read further, slow the clocks

cap.n1: Slow down its clocks. Llama 2 learned to read on texts|of up to about 4,000 tokens,|the word pieces a model reads.|Fine-tuned with a trick called YaRN, it reads 128,000.
cap.n2: Attention compares every word with every other word,|but on its own it can't see order.|The cat chased the dog; the dog chased the cat:|same words, same bag.|So every model has to tell attention where each word sits.
cap.n3: Her slide shows how the answers changed.|The 2017 Transformer added a pattern|of sines and cosines to each word.|GPT-2 and GPT-3 learned one position vector per slot,|and added that.|T5 added a learned nudge inside attention, by distance.
cap.n4: Then, from a 2021 paper by Su and colleagues:|rotary position embedding, RoPE.|LLaMA and Llama 2 use it.
cap.n5: Notice what the first three have in common. They add.
cap.c31: But when you add another thing, then it doesn't really work.
cap.n6: Pour the position into the word,|and the two are mixed for good.|When attention multiplies two mixed vectors,|word-times-position cross terms appear,|and the clean sense of distance gets blurred.
cap.n8: Cut the query and the key into pairs of numbers.|Each pair is an arrow on a dial.|A word at position one turns its arrow one step,|position two, two steps, and so on.
cap.c27: So each of these two were rotated by an angle.
cap.n9: Here is her example. In "we know that",|"we" is at position zero and "know" at one.|So "we" turns zero steps, and "know" turns one.
cap.n10: Now "of course we know".|"We" is at two, "know" at three.|Both arrows turn further, but by the same extra amount.|The angle between them stays the same.
cap.n11: That is the property she wants.
cap.c24: We want the whole embedding to be rotational invariant.
cap.n12: Attention scores two arrows by how well they line up,|and that depends only on the angle between them.|Same two words, one step apart:|the same score at 0 and 1, at 2 and 3, or at 100 and 101.|Only the words and their distance count.
cap.n13: On her next slide, this is one big matrix:|a sine-and-cosine turn for each pair, zeros everywhere else.|It multiplies the query and the key.|Nothing is added, so there are no cross terms.
cap.n14: One more change. The 2017 model added its position once,|at the bottom of a deep stack.|Pass it up through many layers, and, as she puts it,
cap.c22: this kind of positional information will get lost.
cap.n15: So LLaMA applies RoPE inside every attention layer,|to the queries and the keys.|The values are not turned.
cap.c12: And so indeed, this kind of positional encoding|is applied per layer per head.
cap.n16: Not every pair turns at the same speed.|In Llama 2's smallest model, each head holds 128 numbers:|64 pairs, 64 clocks.
cap.n17: The fastest turns about 57 degrees per token:|it tells neighbours apart.|The slowest needs about 54,000 tokens for a single turn:|it tells near from far.
cap.n18: Now the problem. Trained on 4,096 tokens,|the slowest clock never turned more than about 27 degrees.|Feed it 128,000 tokens, and it spins more than twice around:|angles the model has never seen.
cap.n19: Then the fix is plain: slow the clocks down.
cap.n20: Position Interpolation, from Chen and colleagues in 2023,|squeezes the positions.|Every clock runs slower by the same factor,|so a long text fits inside the angles the model knows.|From 4,096 to about 128,000, that is a squeeze of 32.
cap.n21: They stretched LLaMA from 2,048 to 32,768|tokens within 1,000 fine-tuning steps.|The catch: the fast clocks get squeezed too,|and neighbours start to look alike.
cap.n22: A 2023 community post, NTK-aware scaling, split the job.|Leave the fast clocks almost alone,|so neighbours still look like neighbours,|and slow the slow clocks the most.|It works even without fine-tuning.
cap.n23: YaRN, by Peng and colleagues,|refines that split and adds a|temperature to the attention scores.|It needs about 10 times fewer|training tokens than earlier methods,|and it took Llama 2 to 128,000.
cap.n24: Her table's last column runs up to a million and more:|a rough community range, not a measured limit.
cap.c28: So it's kind of a lot of tricks to do it.
cap.n25: One honest limit.|Reading a long text is not the same as using it.|A 2024 test of 17 long-context models found only|about half still did well at 32,000 tokens,|though all of them claimed 32,000 or more.
cap.n26: So: position as a rotation.|Turn the query and the key by their place,|and the angle between them carries the distance.|To read further, slow the clocks.
